meta.descriptionEn: In November 2020, a helicopter crew counting bighorn sheep over a remote Utah canyon spotted something that did not belong: a gleaming metal pillar, firmly planted in the red rock. No one knew who put it there or why. Within days the internet had found it, crowds had reached it, and then, just as suddenly, it was gone. Copies began appearing across the world. This documentary follows the monolith from its secret installation and surprise discovery to the night it was toppled, the theories about artists and aliens, and the strange viral wave it set off. Who made it, and why did the whole internet go wild?
meta.descriptionUr: November 2020 mein Utah ke ek door daraz canyon ke upar helicopter se bighorn sheep ginte hue ek team ko ajeeb cheez nazar aayi: surkh pattharon mein gara hua chamakta hua dhaati sutoon. Kisi ko nahi pata tha ke ise kis ne lagaya aur kyun. Chand dinon mein internet ne ise dhoond liya, log wahan pahunch gaye, aur phir yeh achanak ghayab ho gaya. Is documentary mein dekhein ke yeh monolith kahan se aaya, kis ne ise giraya, aur duniya bhar mein iski nakalen kyun ban gayin.

articleEn: It was the night of 27 November 2020. In the dark of the Utah desert, four people walked toward a shining metal column in a narrow canyon. Others were standing nearby, watching. Then the four pushed. According to one witness, it may have taken about three big shoves to bring the column down. After that, they broke it apart and carried the pieces away in a wheelbarrow. The whole event lasted roughly eight minutes.

The column stood 9.5 feet tall, and for more than four years almost nobody had laid eyes on it. Then the whole world started talking about it. The questions piled up. Who made it? When and why was it put there? And how did one silent column shake the world? The biggest question of all is still open: as of 2026, nobody knows who built it or what they intended.

In this story, we look at how the column was found during a helicopter survey and what it really was. We look at how its name, monolith, connects to the film 2001: A Space Odyssey, and how the internet tracked down its location. We also consider which artists were named as possible makers, and finally how the column disappeared. So let's begin this strange tale, which started with a helicopter flying through the sky.

articleEn: On 18 November 2020, a helicopter was flying low over desert rock in San Juan County, Utah. It was not looking for anything mysterious. On board were officers from the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, who were surveying wild bighorn sheep. The helicopter belonged to the Utah Department of Public Safety and was flown by pilot Bret Hutchings.

Below them lay a long, remote slot canyon. Suddenly a wildlife biologist spotted something metallic and asked the pilot to circle back. Hutchings later told a local news channel that the biologist said, "Whoa, whoa, whoa, turn around, turn around!" Surprised, Hutchings asked, "What?" The biologist replied that there was something strange down there and they had to go and look. Hutchings said it looked man-made and firmly planted in the ground. In his words, it was almost the strangest thing he had seen in all his years of flying. He said the crew joked that if one of them suddenly vanished, the rest should run.

The place was extremely remote, with no parking, no restrooms and no cell phone service. So why were wildlife surveyors flying there? The reason is bighorn sheep. The bighorn (Ovis canadensis) is North America's own wild sheep, named for its large, curved horns. A pair of horns can weigh up to 14 kg, and the whole animal usually weighs up to 143 kg.

About 750,000 years ago these sheep crossed the Bering Land Bridge from Siberia into North America, and their numbers eventually reached the millions. They also became part of Native American mythology. But things changed, and by 1900 only a few thousand were left. The causes were diseases carried by European livestock and excessive hunting. Bighorn sheep are also seen as a good sign of healthy land. So an animal affected by human activity ended up leading a survey crew to a completely unexpected object.

That was only the beginning. What they had seen would soon be in news around the world. The next question was simple: what was this column? Was it art, a prank, or something else? The answer begins with how it was built.

articleEn: So what exactly was it? Start with the size. The column rose about 9.5 feet, or 2.9 meters, from the rock surface. It was not an ordinary column. It had three sides, making it a triangular prism with an equilateral triangle as its base. Each side of the triangle was about 1.9 feet (0.58 meters) long, and its altitude was about 1.67 feet (0.51 meters). Picture it: a base under two feet on each side, rising nearly 2.9 meters. A narrow, tall, metallic tower.

It looked as if it were made from sheets of stainless steel or aluminum, each only 1/8 inch, or 3 millimeters, thick. The sheets were joined with blind rivets. The inside was hollow, and the column was not magnetic. Silicone caulk or epoxy had also been applied around its base, so besides the metal sheets another material was used. Put together, it was a long, slim, three-sided column built from metal sheets. According to one early visitor, when you knocked on it, it sounded like a cardboard box.

Here is another interesting detail. Dave Sparks of the reality series Diesel Brothers went there and posted a video on Instagram. According to him, the builders used a concrete saw to cut into the red rock and set the column in, and some over-cuts from the saw can be seen below it. Wendy Wischer of the University of Utah said that no single person could have done this work and that a group must be behind it. In her view, humor and mystery were part of it too, because most artists want credit for their work.

Now to the name. Utah DPS first called it a monolith, and other media outlets repeated the word. Oddly, the word monolith really means one single huge stone, while this column was made of metal sheets, not stone. Even so, the word stuck. Today it is also tied to the famous Monolith of the film 2001: A Space Odyssey, which the column generally resembled. The name spread quickly. But what is the film's Monolith, and how does it relate to Arthur C. Clarke's stories? That comes next.

articleEn: The original Monolith comes from fiction. In Arthur C. Clarke's Space Odyssey series, Monoliths are machines built as black cuboids. Their sides are in the exact proportion 1:4:9, the squares of 1, 2 and 3, a ratio that is still debated today. In the story, they were built by an unseen extraterrestrial species that Clarke called the Firstborn. According to Clarke, they were perhaps among the oldest intelligent species in the Milky Way, and the story places thousands of other Monoliths across the galaxy.

The first Monolith is found by australopithecines four million years ago, and in the story it sparks their ability to use tools and weapons. The one found in Tycho Crater on the Moon is called TMA-1, buried about 15 meters below the surface. TMA-2 is found near Jupiter and carries Dave Bowman through a star-gate beyond the universe as we know it. All this is the fiction of the film and novels, not reality.

In the film, the first design for the 2001 Monolith was not a black slab. It was a tetrahedral pyramid, taken from the 1951 story The Sentinel. A London firm was asked for a 12-foot plexiglass pyramid, but because of construction problems it suggested a flat slab instead, and Kubrick agreed. On set, though, Kubrick disliked the glass-like look of the prop. Art director Anthony Masters then suggested making the Monolith black, and that is how the famous black slab appeared.

The discarded acrylic Monolith was hung at St Katharine Docks in London in 1977 and can still be seen. Replicas followed the film. In 1973 a black bronze Monolith about 5 meters tall was set up on the University of Hawaii at Mānoa campus, and it still stands. A replica was put up at the Hackers at Large conference in 2001. In June 2020 a 4.5-meter wooden replica was found at the École normale supérieure in Paris. In October 2023 an ultra black 1:4:9 replica appeared at an ESTEC open day. The shape has been fascinating people for decades.

So why was the Utah column called a monolith? The reason is simple: Utah DPS used the word the very first time, and other outlets repeated it. The Utah column was not black, was made of metal sheets, and had a triangular prism shape. Still, its general resemblance to the film was strong enough that the name stuck. But the real question remained: where was this column?

articleEn: How did the public find out about it? On 20 November, Utah DPS posted a photo of the column on Instagram. On 23 November, DPS released videos of it on its website. The location was not given, because of safety concerns. The reason is easy to understand. The place was very remote, with no parking, no restrooms and no cell phone service, and one mistake could put someone in danger.

But the internet does not stop. Within a day, Reddit user Tim Slane found the column on Google Earth. He tracked the helicopter's flight path and matched it with the DPS videos, so the secret was unlocked by clues in those very videos. Slane told The Verge that clues such as the height of the rocks, the erosion pattern in the canyon and the even floor helped him. The even floor suggested that flash floods did not often reach the spot, and the place might be near the upper part of a watershed. It was a small scientific detective story.

The site is called Lockhart Basin, in San Juan County, Utah. Not long after the column was installed, the area became part of Bears Ears National Monument. Now the second question: when was it put there? According to Maxar satellite images, it appeared between 7 July 2016 and 21 October 2016. Google Earth images also show the scrub vegetation around it cleared, so someone had worked there. The date is only estimated from satellite images. The column went up within a window of about three and a half months, and the exact date is unknown.

Another surprising point: for more than four years nobody noticed it. Until November 2020 it stood quietly in the same canyon. It had been placed illegally on public land, so this was a matter of law, not only curiosity. Within 48 hours of the DPS announcement, ordinary people had reached the column and put photos and videos on social media. Within a few days, others had found the place using GPS mapping software. The secret location was out in the open.

Think about it: a place without parking or mobile signal was crowded within days. That was the power of social media. So now we had a location and an approximate date. But the biggest question was still there. Who went to such trouble to put this column there?

articleEn: So who put it there? Many art critics and online users first looked toward the artist John McCracken. He lived in the southwestern United States, believed in extraterrestrial life, and liked the idea of leaving an artwork behind in the desert. His own metallic monoliths were similar in spirit. New York gallerist David Zwirner called the column "nearly identical" to McCracken's 2011 work Fair, a piece Zwirner himself displays, so his statement carried weight. But a Zwirner spokesman later withdrew the first statement. He told The Guardian it was probably another artist's tribute to McCracken. Resemblance and authorship are not the same thing. The column looked like McCracken's work, but that did not mean he was behind it.

A second name raised was Petecia Le Fawnhawk, who lives in Utah and has placed sculptures in desert locations. She denied it. Then a collective called The Most Famous Artist first took credit for placing the column, but later admitted it was not their work. Was it a film set? According to the Utah Film Commission, as far as they knew, the column was not part of any film production.

So four main paths had appeared: a famous artist, a local sculptor, a collective and a film production. None of the four was confirmed. Remember also that, according to Dave Sparks, the column was set into red rock with a concrete saw, which means the work was done with proper tools. Wendy Wischer of the University of Utah said one person could not have done it, and that a group was behind it. She added that most artists want recognition, but here humor and mystery seemed part of the intention.

It is important to remember that these are all theories. No name has been confirmed, and several ended with denials or retractions. Even after all the research and debate, as of 2026, the simplest question has no answer: who, and why? The New York Times wrote that its unknown origin gave a pleasing feeling of uncertainty, and that if the maker were known, the column might lose its aura and power. But once the location was known, the crowds became a bigger problem than the mystery. In the next part we see what the crowds left behind.

articleEn: As soon as the monolith's location became known, people set out from far and wide toward the lonely spot. Within 48 hours of the Utah DPS announcement, they had arrived and were posting photos and videos on social media. The site was not easy to reach, with no parking, no restrooms and no cell phone service. Even so, hundreds of people came, according to reports. It was suddenly a lot of pressure on one small canyon.

The Bureau of Land Management, or BLM, which manages the site, expressed clear displeasure. It said visitors had left human waste and other trash and had parked vehicles on vegetation. It warned that the site could not handle so many visitors arriving suddenly. Local people also feared that more foot traffic could damage Native American sites and artifacts, including petroglyphs, which are carvings on rock. They worried that growing visitor numbers could harm such historic marks.

On 23 November 2020, BLM issued a statement saying that putting up any structure on public lands without permission, even art, is illegal. It included a memorable line: the law applies "no matter what planet you're from." The Utah Department of Heritage & Arts also voiced concern on Facebook, saying that installing the monolith could have damaged the area's archeological artifacts. It said the monolith's craftsmanship was better than graffiti, but it was still vandalism, and in its words it had altered the natural environment in a way that could not be undone. articleEn: On the night of 27 November 2020, at about 8:40 pm, a group arrived at the monolith. According to photographer Ross Bernards, other people were there too, watching the scene. Bernards said the group began pushing the monolith as soon as they arrived, using their full body weight. In his words, it probably took about three big shoves to bring it down. And so a column that had stood for more than four years came to the ground.

After it fell, the group said this is why you do not leave trash in the desert, and they repeated the words "leave no trace." Then they broke the structure apart and carried the pieces off in a wheelbarrow. Bernards said the whole job took only eight minutes. One thing was left behind: the triangular top piece, which was also gone later. At first the identity of the four was unknown, but several witnesses posted details and pictures of the dismantling online.

Was it theft? BLM denied any involvement and said the monolith was private property, leaving further investigation to the local sheriff's office. On 29 November, the San Juan County Sheriff's Office said it did not have the resources. The same office also posted a "Most Wanted" list on Facebook featuring several aliens. But on 30 November that changed. Authorities announced a joint investigation with BLM, and chief deputy Alan Freestone said there were some leads. There was a legal obstacle, though. Authorities could not make it a stolen property case, because nobody had claimed ownership of the monolith.

On 1 December, Andy Lewis took responsibility in a video on YouTube. Sylvan Christensen shared the same video on TikTok and Instagram that day. According to the group, they acted because the environmental damage to the area from visitors and tourists troubled them. They later said they had heard online rumors that some people planned to destroy the monolith, so, in their account, they removed it before anyone else arrived.

The reaction was harsh all the same. The group received hateful comments and threats. Some people did not like what they called protecting the environment. A few weeks later, Lewis posted another video on Instagram showing the monolith reassembled in his backyard. Finally, on 18 December, Lewis handed the structure over to the Bureau of Land Management. It had been with him for about a month. Lewis hoped that after the investigations ended, the monolith would find a new home. But did the story of monoliths stop there?

articleEn: The Utah monolith was gone, but the story was not over. Right after its discovery, similar columns began appearing around the world. They showed up in other parts of North America, and in several countries in Europe and Australia. In many places, local artists deliberately built them as copies of the Utah monolith, and some came forward to name it as their inspiration. Other monoliths were put up by small businesses for promotional purposes, so a mysterious object was also copied for commercial ends.

CNN called it the viral art moment of the year, while Vox compared the monoliths to a living meme. The numbers were not small either: by June 2024, at least 245 similar structures had appeared worldwide. Now back to the original Utah monolith. As of 2026, the identity and purpose of its makers are still unknown. We do not know who put it there or why. Satellite images show that it appeared between July and October 2016.

One lesson of this story concerns public land. A mysterious object drew so much attention that hundreds of people reached a remote canyon, and the land paid the price. Trash, vehicles parked on vegetation, and worries for archeological sites were the result of the crowds. Meanwhile, media coverage was so intense that the monolith became an international topic and a wave of online speculation began. One view is that anonymity was its attraction, and The New York Times wrote that if the answer were known, it might lose its aura.

So what questions remain open? Who put it up? Why? And could a similar column suddenly appear somewhere again? One thing is certain: a 9.5-foot triangular prism made of sheets just 1/8 inch thick drew the attention of the whole world. Andy Lewis and his companions said they wanted to protect the environment, while some people sharply criticized their method. The story shows that remote places can change within days after a viral news story, which is why the leave no trace principle matters.
